## formal
Let $N \ge 1$ and let $L_{N} = \Cl(N, N{+}2)$ be the tower level with orthogonal generators $e_{0}, e_{1}, e_{2}, e_{3}$ ($Q = +1, -1, -1, -1$) and the tower planes $(e_{j}', f_{j}')$, $Q(e_{j}') = 1$, $Q(f_{j}') = -1$, $j = 1, \dots, N - 1$ (floor $N - 1$ of the tower on $\Cl(1,3)$, Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies}), read through the Witt decomposition of its vector space: the anisotropic kernel $\mathrm{span}\{e_{2}, e_{3}\}$, of signature $(0,2)$, orthogonal to $N$ hyperbolic (transport) planes, the radial plane $(e_{0}, e_{1})$ (mode $0$) and the tower planes (modes $1, \dots, N - 1$). $B_{N}$ is the subalgebra generated by the $2N$ plane generators. For a plane $(e, f)$, $v = \tfrac12(e + f) = a^{*}$, $w = \tfrac12(e - f) = a$, $n = vw$, $\omega = ef$; $\Gamma = \prod_{\text{planes}}\omega$; $J = e_{2}e_{3}$; $\sigma = e_{0}e_{1}$; $I_{4} = e_{0}e_{1}e_{2}e_{3}$; $I_{n}$ is the product of all $2N + 2$ generators in the order listed; $*$ is the frame adjoint of Theorem \claimref{tower.structure-tower-c-norms} on the real level (the antiautomorphism fixing the generators of square $+1$ and negating those of square $-1$).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(No unit in the hyperbolic tower.)} In $\Cl(N,N)$, generated by $N$ hyperbolic planes alone, the commutant of the even subalgebra is $\mathrm{span}\{1, \Gamma\}$, $\Gamma^{2} = +1$, and $(\alpha + \beta\Gamma)^{2} = \alpha^{2} + \beta^{2} + 2\alpha\beta\Gamma$: no element that commutes with every even element squares to $-1$. Inside the transport algebra, self-adjoint boson fields (even elements) have no unit that commutes with all bosonic elements.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(The kernel bivector.)} In $L_{N}$, $J^{2} = -1$, $J^{*} = -J$, and $J$ commutes with every plane generator, hence with all of $B_{N}$ (every mode $v_{j}, w_{j}$ and every pair); $J = I_{4}\sigma$.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The commutant of transport is a quaternion algebra.)} The commutant of $B_{N}$ in $L_{N}$ is $\mathrm{span}\{1, J, \Gamma e_{2}, \Gamma e_{3}\}$, with $(\Gamma e_{2})^{2} = (\Gamma e_{3})^{2} = -1$ and $(\Gamma e_{2})(\Gamma e_{3}) = J = -(\Gamma e_{3})(\Gamma e_{2})$: a quaternion algebra, the twisted copy of the ground $\Cl(0,2)$. Its even part is $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$, and $\pm J$ are its only even elements of square $-1$; they are also its only units fixed by the rotors $e^{\varphi J}$ of the kernel plane, which turn $(\Gamma e_{2}, \Gamma e_{3})$ through $2\varphi$. In the tower's limit only $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$ commutes with every plane (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.plane-commutant-even-ground}(i) with ground signature $(0,2)$). The uniqueness needs the radial plane among the transport planes: if $(e_{0}, e_{1})$ is counted in the ground $\Cl(1,3)$ and only the tower planes as transport ($N \ge 2$), the even part of their commutant is $\Cl^{+}(1,3)$ (of dimension $8$), which contains $I_{4}$, $J$, $e_{1}e_{2}$ and $e_{1}e_{3}$, all of square $-1$; then $J$ and $I_{4} = J\sigma$ both commute with transport.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The level pseudoscalar.)} $I_{n} = J\Gamma$, $I_{n}^{2} = -1$, $I_{n}^{*} = -I_{n}$; $\Gamma^{*} = \Gamma = \prod_{j}(1 - 2n_{j})$, the fermion parity, which anticommutes with every $v_{j}, w_{j}$ and commutes with every product of two. Hence $I_{n}\tfrac12(1 \pm \Gamma) = \pm J\tfrac12(1 \pm \Gamma)$: $I_{n} = J$ on even and $-J$ on odd fermion number. $\operatorname{Ad}(I_{n})$ is the grade involution of $L_{N}$, which on $B_{N}$ is $\operatorname{Ad}(\Gamma)$. $I_{n}$ and $J$ are not identified.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Hermitian boson fields with unit $J$.)} For every $X \in B_{N}$, $\phi_{X} = X + X^{*}$ and $\pi_{X} = J(X^{*} - X)$ are self-adjoint and $[\phi_{X}, \pi_{X}] = 2J[X, X^{*}]$; for $X, Y \in B_{N}$ with $[X, Y] = 0$, $[\phi_{X}, \pi_{Y}] = J([X, Y^{*}] + [Y, X^{*}])$ and $[\phi_{X}, \phi_{Y}] = [\pi_{X}, \pi_{Y}] = [X, Y^{*}] - [Y, X^{*}]$.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Collective pairs.} For $N = 2M$ and $S = \sum_{k=0}^{M-1}v_{2k}w_{2k+1}$, $\phi = \phi_{S}$, $\pi = \pi_{S}$: $[\phi, \pi] = 2J\sum_{k}(n_{2k} - n_{2k+1})$ exactly. With $P_{\mathrm{pol}} = \prod_{k}n_{2k}(1 - n_{2k+1})$, $SP_{\mathrm{pol}} = 0$, $X_{j} = (S^{*})^{j}P_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is nonzero for $j \le M$ and zero for $j = M + 1$, and $[\phi, \pi]X_{j} = 2(M - 2j)JX_{j}$; so $\Phi = \phi/\sqrt{2M}$, $\Pi = \pi/\sqrt{2M}$ satisfy $[\Phi, \Pi]X_{j} = (1 - 2j/M)JX_{j}$: the Hermitian canonical relation $[\Phi, \Pi] = J$ holds exactly on the polarised element and, at fixed $j$, as $M \to \infty$.
\item \emph{Density modes.} On a window of the $N$ modes, $\rho_{q} = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1-q}v_{k}w_{k+q}$ ($1 \le q \le N - 1$) satisfy $[\rho_{q}, \rho_{q'}] = 0$ and $[\phi_{\rho_{q}}, \pi_{\rho_{q}}] = 2J(\sum_{k<q}n_{k} - \sum_{k \ge N-q}n_{k})$; for $2q \le N$ and $E_{q} = \prod_{k<q}n_{k}\prod_{k \ge N-q}(1 - n_{k})$ (the filled sea's edge-clean projector), $[\phi_{\rho_{q}}, \pi_{\rho_{q}}]\psi = 2qJ\psi$ whenever $E_{q}\psi = \psi$.
\item \emph{Lemma.} In any real $*$-algebra, let $u^{2} = -1$, $u^{*} = -u$, and let $u$ commute with a family $X_{q}$ with $[X_{q}, X_{q'}] = 0$ and $[X_{q}, X_{q'}^{*}] = c_{q}\delta_{qq'}$, $c_{q} > 0$ real. Then $\Phi_{q} = (X_{q} + X_{q}^{*})/\sqrt{2c_{q}}$ and $\Pi_{q} = u(X_{q}^{*} - X_{q})/\sqrt{2c_{q}}$ are self-adjoint and $[\Phi_{q}, \Pi_{q'}] = u\,\delta_{qq'}$, $[\Phi_{q}, \Phi_{q'}] = [\Pi_{q}, \Pi_{q'}] = 0$. The canonical relations of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.fluctuation-forms-of-the-tower-and-density-wave-bosons-of-the-null-vacuum}(vi) on its domain $\mathcal{D}$ have this form with $X_{q} = \rho_{q}$, $c_{q} = q$, and $u$ any unit commuting with the band modes there.
\end{itemize}
\item[(vi)] \emph{(The sign of $J$ and the phase circle.)} The map $\alpha$ with $e_{3} \mapsto -e_{3}$ and every other generator fixed extends to a $*$-automorphism of $L_{N}$; it fixes $B_{N}$ pointwise and $\sigma$, and sends $J \mapsto -J$, $I_{4} \mapsto -I_{4}$, $I_{n} \mapsto -I_{n}$, $(\phi_{X}, \pi_{X}) \mapsto (\phi_{X}, -\pi_{X})$. So nothing in the transport algebra fixes the sign of $J$; given $\sigma$, it is the orientation of $I_{4}$ ($J = I_{4}\sigma$). With $Q = \sum_{k}(n_{2k} - n_{2k+1})$ and $U_{\theta} = e^{\theta JQ/2} = \prod_{k}(1 - n_{2k} + n_{2k}e^{\theta J/2})(1 - n_{2k+1} + n_{2k+1}e^{-\theta J/2})$, $U_{\theta}$ is unitary, $U_{\theta}SU_{\theta}^{*} = e^{\theta J}S$, and $(\phi, \pi) \mapsto (\phi\cos\theta - \pi\sin\theta, \phi\sin\theta + \pi\cos\theta)$, which keeps $[\phi, \pi]$. The phase $e^{\theta J} = \cos\theta + J\sin\theta$ has period $2\pi$; it is the rotor of the kernel plane, $\operatorname{Ad}(e^{\theta J})$ turns $e_{2}, e_{3}$ through $2\theta$ and fixes $B_{N}$ pointwise, and $e^{\pi J} = -1$ is the rotor of the turn by $2\pi$.
\end{enumerate}
Clauses (i) to (vi) are proved. \emph{Reading (argued).} The orientation of $I_{4}$ relative to time is the datum that Premise (N$_{+}$) assumes (\claimref{synthesis.n-plus-null-ground-state}); by (vi), with $\sigma$ fixed, it is the sign of $J$, which now orients both the fermion phase flow $v \mapsto e^{-Jt}v$ of \claimref{synthesis.transverse-bivector-is-the-complex-unit-of-the-radial-atom}(iv) and the boson relation $[\Phi, \Pi] = +J$ of (v): reversing it reverses both together.

## technical
A boson field written as a self-adjoint pair needs a unit: something that squares to $-1$, is anti-self-adjoint, and commutes with the fields. The tower's hyperbolic planes alone do not supply one. In $\Cl(N,N)$ the elements commuting with every even element are $\alpha + \beta\Gamma$, with $\Gamma$ the product of the plane volume elements, and these square to $\alpha^{2} + \beta^{2} + 2\alpha\beta\Gamma$, never $-1$. A tower level over spacetime is $\Cl(N, N{+}2)$, whose vector space is $N$ hyperbolic planes, the radial plane among them, plus a two-dimensional kernel of square $-1$. The kernel bivector $J = e_{2}e_{3}$ squares to $-1$, is anti-self-adjoint, and commutes with every mode operator. The whole commutant of the transport algebra is a quaternion algebra $\mathrm{span}\{1, J, \Gamma e_{2}, \Gamma e_{3}\}$, and $\pm J$ is its only even unit, the one the kernel rotations fix, and the only one surviving in the tower's limit. The level pseudoscalar is $I_{n} = J\Gamma$, which equals $J$ on even and $-J$ on odd fermion number; the two are not identified. With $J$, any transport element $X$ gives the self-adjoint fields $\phi = X + X^{*}$ and $\pi = J(X^{*} - X)$, and $[\phi, \pi] = 2J[X, X^{*}]$. For the collective hopping pair $S$ of $M$ blocks this is $2J$ times the edge count $\sum(n_{2k} - n_{2k+1})$, so the normalised fields satisfy $[\Phi, \Pi] = (1 - 2j/M)J$ on the $j$-th rung of the polarised ladder; for density modes of a window it is $2qJ$ on the filled sea's edge-clean projector. A lemma gives the full Hermitian canonical relations for any family of commuting canonical pairs and any commuting unit. Uniqueness of $J$ depends on counting the radial plane as a transport plane: with the radial plane in the ground, the even commutant of the tower planes is the even spacetime algebra, where $I_{4}$ (the field theory's unit) and $J$ both serve. Finally, reflecting $e_{3}$ is an automorphism that fixes every transport element and reverses $J$ and $I_{4}$ together, so the sign of $J$ is not fixed by the fermions; given the radial plane's orientation it is the orientation of $I_{4}$, the datum Premise (N$_{+}$) assumes. The boson phase circle is $e^{\theta J}$, implemented inside the level by $e^{\theta JQ/2}$; it is the kernel plane's rotor, and its value $-1$ at $\theta = \pi$ is the rotor of a full turn.

## lay
Quantum fields that describe bosons, the particles that can share a state, are usually written as pairs of real quantities whose commutator is the imaginary unit. The graph builds everything from fermions living in a tower of planes, so it has to find that unit inside its own algebra. The planes alone have none: nothing that commutes with all their pairs squares to minus one. The extra two directions of spacetime that are not part of any plane, the two directions along a horizon's sphere, supply one: the product of those two directions squares to minus one and commutes with every fermion operation. It is the only such element of the right type, it is what survives at the top of the tower, and with it the collective pairs of fermions give boson fields with the standard commutator, exactly in the states where the bosons were already known to appear. Its sign is a free choice that nothing among the fermions fixes, and it is the same choice that the series' premise about horizons makes when it fixes the direction of time relative to the imaginary unit.

## one-liner
In the tower level $\Cl(N, N{+}2)$ the commutant of the $N$ hyperbolic planes is the quaternion algebra $\mathrm{span}\{1, J, \Gamma e_{2}, \Gamma e_{3}\}$ with unique even unit $\pm J = \pm e_{2}e_{3}$ (the planes alone have none), $I_{n} = J\Gamma$, and $\phi = X + X^{*}$, $\pi = J(X^{*} - X)$ are self-adjoint with $[\phi, \pi] = 2J[X, X^{*}]$, giving $2J\sum_{k}(n_{2k} - n_{2k+1})$ for collective pairs; the sign of $J$ is fixed by nothing in transport.

proofs.proof-main.tex:
\emph{Two facts used throughout.} (a) For a basis vector $e_{a}$ and a basis blade $e_{B}$ (index set $B$), $e_{a}e_{B} = (-1)^{|B| - [a \in B]}e_{B}e_{a}$: $e_{a}$ anticommutes with each factor of $e_{B}$ other than itself (Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.orthogonal-anticommute}) and commutes with itself. (b) Conjugation by a basis blade maps every basis blade to plus or minus itself: by the product formula of Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.orthogonal-anticommute}, $e_{E}e_{B} = \pm e_{B}e_{E}$, both products being a sign times $(\prod_{E \cap B}Q)\,e_{E \triangle B}$. Hence if $x = \sum_{B}x_{B}e_{B}$ commutes with $e_{E}$, then $0 = e_{E}x - xe_{E} = \sum_{B}x_{B}(\epsilon_{B} - 1)e_{B}e_{E}$ with $\epsilon_{B} = \pm 1$, and since the $e_{B}e_{E}$ are, up to nonzero factors, distinct basis blades, $x_{B} = 0$ whenever $\epsilon_{B} = -1$. So the commutant of any set of basis blades is spanned by the basis blades that commute with all of them, and the commutant of a set of generators can be computed blade by blade. Every commutant below is the commutant of the algebra generated by a set of basis blades, so (b) applies to each.

\emph{(i).} In $\Cl(N,N)$, $n = 2N \ge 2$, the even subalgebra is spanned by even blades, products of the bivectors $e_{a}e_{b}$, so its commutant is the commutant of the bivectors. By (a), $e_{a}e_{b}e_{B} = (-1)^{2|B| - [a \in B] - [b \in B]}e_{B}e_{a}e_{b}$, so $e_{B}$ commutes with $e_{a}e_{b}$ exactly when $[a \in B] = [b \in B]$. Requiring this for every pair $a \ne b$ forces $B = \emptyset$ or $B = \{1, \dots, n\}$. In the order $e_{1}f_{1}e_{2}f_{2}\cdots$ the full blade is $\prod_{j}\omega_{j} = \Gamma$, which squares to $+1$ (Theorem \claimref{tower.volume-elements-planes}). So the commutant is $\mathrm{span}\{1, \Gamma\}$; it has no odd part. Its even part is the centre of $\Cl^{+}(N,N)$, which agrees with the parenthesis of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.plane-commutant-even-ground}(ii) at $r = 0$ ($\omega^{2} = (-1)^{r/2} = 1$). For real $\alpha, \beta$, $(\alpha + \beta\Gamma)^{2} = \alpha^{2} + \beta^{2} + 2\alpha\beta\Gamma$; equal to $-1$ would need $\alpha^{2} + \beta^{2} = -1$. The script checks (b) on all pairs of blades and computes the commutant of the bivectors for $N = 1, 2, 3$, and the square at four rational points.

\emph{(ii).} $J^{2} = e_{2}e_{3}e_{2}e_{3} = -e_{2}^{2}e_{3}^{2} = -1$. The $*$ of Theorem \claimref{tower.structure-tower-c-norms}, restricted to the real level, is the antiautomorphism with $x^{*} = x$ for generators of square $+1$ and $x^{*} = -x$ for those of square $-1$; on a blade it is reversion times $(-1)^{\#\{\text{factors of square } -1\}}$. So $J^{*} = e_{3}^{*}e_{2}^{*} = e_{3}e_{2} = -J$, $v^{*} = \tfrac12(e - f) = w$, and the ladder pairs satisfy the CAR (Theorem \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors}; directly, $\{w_{j}, v_{k}\} = \tfrac14\{e_{j} - f_{j}, e_{k} + f_{k}\} = \tfrac12(Q(e_{j}) - Q(f_{j}))\delta_{jk} = \delta_{jk}$ and $\{v_{j}, v_{k}\} = \{w_{j}, w_{k}\} = 0$ since $v_{j}, w_{j}$ are null and orthogonal to the other planes). Every plane generator is orthogonal to $e_{2}$ and $e_{3}$, so anticommutes with each and commutes with $J$; $J$ therefore commutes with $B_{N}$. $I_{4}\sigma = e_{0}e_{1}e_{2}e_{3}e_{0}e_{1}$; moving $e_{0}e_{1}$ to the left past $e_{2}e_{3}$ costs four transpositions, so $I_{4}\sigma = \sigma\sigma J = \sigma^{2}J$, and $\sigma^{2} = e_{0}e_{1}e_{0}e_{1} = -e_{0}^{2}e_{1}^{2} = 1$: $J = I_{4}\sigma$, as in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.transverse-bivector-is-the-complex-unit-of-the-radial-atom}(i). The script checks the CAR, $v^{*} = w$, the antiautomorphism property on all blade pairs for $N \le 2$, and the rest for $N = 1, 2, 3$.

\emph{(iii).} Let $P$ be the set of the $2N$ plane indices and $K = \{2, 3\}$. By (b) the commutant of $B_{N}$ (that of its generators) is spanned by the blades $e_{B}$ with, by (a), $|B| - [a \in B]$ even for every $a \in P$. If $B$ contained one plane index and missed another, $|B| - 1$ and $|B|$ would both be even; so $B \cap P = \emptyset$ or $B \supseteq P$. In the first case $B \subseteq K$ with $|B|$ even: $B = \emptyset$ or $K$, giving $1$ and $J$. In the second $|B|$ is odd, $|B| = 2N + |B \cap K|$, so $|B \cap K| = 1$: $B = P \cup \{2\}$ or $P \cup \{3\}$. Since $\Gamma = \pm e_{P}$, these blades are $\pm\Gamma e_{2}$ and $\pm\Gamma e_{3}$. So the commutant is $\mathrm{span}\{1, J, \Gamma e_{2}, \Gamma e_{3}\}$, of dimension $4$. By Theorem \claimref{tower.volume-elements-planes}, $\Gamma^{2} = 1$ and $\Gamma$ commutes with the non-plane generators $e_{2}$, $e_{3}$, so $(\Gamma e_{2})^{2} = \Gamma^{2}e_{2}^{2} = -1$, likewise $(\Gamma e_{3})^{2} = -1$, $(\Gamma e_{2})(\Gamma e_{3}) = e_{2}e_{3} = J$ and $(\Gamma e_{3})(\Gamma e_{2}) = e_{3}e_{2} = -J$: the quaternion relations. This is the twisted copy $A$ of Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies} for ground $\Cl(0,2)$ with the $N$ planes, generated by $e_{2}\Gamma$ and $e_{3}\Gamma$. A general element $q = a + bJ + c\,\Gamma e_{2} + d\,\Gamma e_{3}$ has $q^{2} = a^{2} - b^{2} - c^{2} - d^{2} + 2a(bJ + c\,\Gamma e_{2} + d\,\Gamma e_{3})$, the three units anticommuting pairwise, so $q^{2} = -1$ exactly when $a = 0$ and $b^{2} + c^{2} + d^{2} = 1$. $\Gamma e_{2}$ and $\Gamma e_{3}$ have odd grade $2N + 1$, so the even part is $\mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$ and its units are $\pm J$. For the kernel rotor $R = e^{\varphi J} = \cos\varphi + J\sin\varphi$ (Theorem \claimref{std-algebra.bivector-exponential}), $J$ is fixed, while $\Gamma e_{2}$, $\Gamma e_{3}$ anticommute with $J$ ($Je_{2} = -e_{2}J$, $\Gamma$ commutes with $J$), so $R(\Gamma e_{2})R^{-1} = R^{2}\Gamma e_{2} = \cos 2\varphi\,\Gamma e_{2} + \sin 2\varphi\,J\Gamma e_{2}$ and $J\Gamma e_{2} = \Gamma e_{3}$: a turn through $2\varphi$ of the plane $(\Gamma e_{2}, \Gamma e_{3})$. A unit $bJ + c\,\Gamma e_{2} + d\,\Gamma e_{3}$ is fixed by every such $R$ exactly when $c = d = 0$. The limit: Theorem \claimref{synthesis.plane-commutant-even-ground}(i), for ground signature $(p, q) = (0, 2)$ ($n = 2 \ge 1$), gives the commutant of all planes in the limit as $\Cl^{0}(0,2) = \mathrm{span}\{1, e_{2}e_{3}\} = \mathrm{span}\{1, J\}$. For $N = 1$ the commutant is the centraliser of $e_{0}, e_{1}$ in $\Cl(1,3)$ stored in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.transverse-bivector-is-the-complex-unit-of-the-radial-atom}(i). The contrast: with ground $\Cl(1,3)$ and transport the $N - 1 \ge 1$ tower planes, the same blade argument (now with $P$ the tower-plane indices and the four ground indices free) gives the blades $e_{B}$ with $B \cap P = \emptyset$, $|B|$ even, or $B \supseteq P$, $|B|$ odd: $2^{3} + 2^{3} = 16$ blades, the twisted copy of $\Cl(1,3)$ of Theorem \claimref{tower.commuting-copies}; its even part is $\Cl^{+}(1,3)$, spanned by $1$, the six bivectors $e_{\mu}e_{\nu}$ and $I_{4}$, of which $e_{1}e_{2}$, $e_{1}e_{3}$, $e_{2}e_{3}$ and $I_{4}$ square to $-1$.     for k in range(M):

    # phase circle: U = prod_k (1 - n_2k + n_2k (c + sJ)) (1 - n_2k+1 + n_2k+1 (c - sJ)) = e^{theta J Q / 2}
